title: Al-Ahad, the Unique
tomorrow: why does one Arabic word need a whole phrase in English?

cards: Everyone has a song on repeat, the one friends beg you to skip. In the time of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, a man had a surah like that.
He was leading a group of travelers in prayer, and every time, whatever else he recited, he finished with the same short surah. Every prayer. The same few lines.
His companions noticed. Then it started to bother them. When they came home, they told the Prophet.
And the Prophet said: go and ask him why.

teach.b: His answer, as Sahih al-Bukhari reports it, was simple: because it describes the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it.
And the Prophet sent back word: tell him that Allah loves him.

Here is the surah he couldn't stop saying, al-Ikhlas, in Pickthall's words: "Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him."
The word for One in that first line is ahad, and today's Name is Al-Ahad, the Unique. Yesterday's Name, Al-Wahid, says there is one.
Some scholars hear Al-Ahad saying something more: one with no parts, nothing to divide, nothing beside Him to set Him next to. Which is why the surah ends where it does. Not with a number.
With none comparable. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight.

teach.h: EQUAL TO A THIRD OF THE QUR'AN.
teach.b: Another report in Bukhari says this short surah is equal to a third of the Qur'an.
Scholars explain that in different ways, and the report itself doesn't stop to say which. The man in the story didn't explain anything.
He loved who the surah described, and that was enough for the Prophet to send him good news.

how: In each unit of prayer Muslims recite al-Fatiha and then other verses of the Qur'an; al-Ikhlas, being short, is a frequent choice, and children often learn it early.

o: the Victor, who stands alone in every battle
the First, who was there before everything
the Unique: one with no parts, none like Him

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: told the Prophet about their leader

s: Al-Ahad and Al-Wahid are two spellings of one Name
they're two Names. some scholars hear Al-Ahad as one with no parts, none comparable.
the Prophet told the man to vary his recitation
he asked why, then sent word: tell him that Allah loves him.
a report in Bukhari calls al-Ikhlas equal to a third of the Qur'an
Sahih al-Bukhari reports it; scholars explain the third in different ways.

games.q: your little cousin plays the same song before every game, and the team teases him. he asks you if he should quit it. what would the travelers' story do first?
o: ask him why he loves it before anyone decides anything.
tell him to stop, since a habit that bugs the team should go.
tell him the team's opinion doesn't matter at all.
games.why: the Prophet scolded no one. he asked the man why, and the reason was love for who the surah describes.

practice: Say al-Ikhlas once, slowly and out loud: in Arabic if you know it, qul huwa Allahu ahad, or in Pickthall's English, He is Allah, the One. Then let the sit hold just that one word, ahad.
When another thought walks in and stands next to it, the test, the group chat, tomorrow, notice it, let it go, and come back to the one word with nothing set beside it.

wordCard.voice: Al-Ahad. The Unique: one without division, none comparable, the Name in al-Ikhlas's first line.

orig.note: Arabic: the Unique, the One. ahad is the word for one in al-Ikhlas's first line.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: unique, the One a traveler loved too much to stop describing. Name sixty-seven, kept.

sources.q: Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 7375 (the leader who ended each recitation with al-Ikhlas: 'tell him that Allah loves him')
Sahih al-Bukhari 5013 (al-Ikhlas equal to a third of the Qur'an)
